x: Every later module assumes you can use a terminal, version your work with git, debug C, rebuild a Python environment and read papers efficiently. Set this up once here so it does not slow you down later. The repo you create holds every module's work. A public GitHub repo ml-compilers-log with a README (goals, schedule, hardware), LOG.md, a modules/ directory, a Makefile target that compiles and runs a sanitized C hello-world, a pytest that passes, and a GitHub Actions CI workflow that runs both on every push. Build a reproducible dev environment for the whole course: a Dockerfile or Nix flake that pins clang, gdb, perf, Python and uv, plus a CI matrix (Linux x86-64 and macOS arm64) that builds and tests every module directory. Measure cold-start setup time on a fresh machine and get it under 10 minutes, documented in the README. Write shell pipelines and small bash scripts, locally and over ssh. Use git branches and tags, and recover from a bad merge with git reflog. Compile C with -g and -fsanitize=address and find a crash with gdb or lldb. Rebuild your Python environment from a lockfile. Read a paper with Keshav's three-pass method and write a five-sentence summary. Write a one-line shell pipeline that prints the 5 largest files under a directory. Explain the difference between a commit, a branch and a tag in git's data model. Use gdb or lldb to find the line of a segfault in a 20-line C program without adding printfs. Recreate your Python environment from scratch on a clean machine (or container) from your lockfile alone. Summarize a paper after Keshav's first pass in five sentences (the five Cs). WSL slow or files missing: keep the repo under ~/ in Linux, not /mnt/c; open it with code . from WSL. macOS 'gdb' won't run: use lldb, which ships with the Xcode Command Line Tools; the commands map almost one to one (lldb's GDB-to-LLDB command map helps). git 'detached HEAD' or a messy merge: run git status and git log --oneline --graph --all before anything else; git reflog can recover almost anything. Limit tooling setup (dotfiles, themes) to two evenings, then start Module 1. Pip and conda in the same env cause mysterious import errors: pick one tool (uv recommended) and one env per project.

x: PyTorch, LLVM, MLIR, CUDA and CUTLASS are written in C++, and later modules ask you to write an LLVM pass, a C++/CUDA array backend and templated GPU kernels. This module teaches the parts of modern C++ those tools use: RAII, move semantics, templates, lambdas, CMake and Python bindings. kiln itself stays in C. (1) A Buffer<T> class template that owns a heap array: rule of five written by hand, then replaced by std::unique_ptr<T[]> with the rule of zero, plus GoogleTest tests that count allocations to prove a move never copies. (2) Extend llvm-tutor's HelloWorld pass to print, for each function, its basic-block count and instruction count, and test it on a C file of your own with opt. Add a float16 element type with a constrained template specialization, and a lazy expression-template Tensor where a + b * c builds an expression tree that evaluates in one fused loop. Benchmark it against the eager version and explain the speedup in memory-traffic terms, as a preview of the fusion you build in Module 16. Write C++20 classes that own resources through RAII, following the rule of zero or the rule of five. Use move semantics and std::unique_ptr to transfer ownership without copies, and prove it with tests. Write function and class templates over a dtype and a compile-time size. Build a C++ library with CMake, test it with GoogleTest and call it from Python through nanobind. Build and run an out-of-tree LLVM pass plugin. Name the five special member functions and say which ones the compiler generates for a class holding a std::unique_ptr member. Explain what std::move does at runtime, and what state a moved-from std::vector is in. Explain why a class template's member functions are usually defined in the header. Show the assembly on Compiler Explorer for a templated add<float> and a hand-written C add_f32, and explain why they match. Your Buffer<T> tests pass under -fsanitize=address,undefined. Linker error undefined reference for a template: the template body is in a .cpp file. Move it to the header. A double free after copying your class: you wrote a destructor but not the copy constructor and copy assignment. Delete them or follow the rule of zero. Calling C from C++ fails to link: wrap the C header's declarations in extern "C" { ... }. CMake cannot find LLVM: pass -DLT_LLVM_INSTALL_DIR=$(llvm-config --prefix) (or your Homebrew LLVM path) and use the same LLVM version that llvm-tutor targets. Template error messages run for pages: read the first error only, and add a C++20 requires clause so the error names the broken constraint.

x: Your BEAM search picked schedules by trial. Two other approaches exist: polyhedral compilers prove which transforms are legal from dependences, and learned auto-schedulers predict runtime with a cost model. This module covers both. islpy-based legality checks for your loop transforms, and a learned cost model that reduces how many schedules BEAM has to measure. Train a single cost model on schedules from two GPUs and show that fine-tuning on 10% of the second GPU's data matches a model trained from scratch on all of it, measured by top-1 schedule runtime on 10 held-out kernels. Add polyhedral legality as a hard filter and report how many sampled schedules it removes. Write loop nests as isl sets and maps and check transform legality from dependences Train and evaluate a learned cost model for schedule search, split by program Your compiler rejects interchanging the loops of a[i][j] = a[i-1][j+1] and accepts interchange on a matmul Cost-model-guided search reaches within 10% of plain BEAM's best runtime using at most 25% of its measurements, on 5 kernels You can write the iteration domain and the tiled schedule of a matmul as isl sets and maps A one-page comparison of the Halide 2019 autoscheduler, Ansor and Pluto: search space, cost model, legality handling isl notation unfamiliar: write each tutorial example by hand first, then check it with isl Cost model looks too good: split train/test by program, not by schedule, or schedules of the same program leak Measurements noisy: lock GPU clocks, warm up, take the median of repeated runs Pluto fails to build: use a container; the tiling hyperplanes are what you need from it
